content:
When Muslims point to passages in which the Bible gives God a human form, Christian apologists often answer that the Quran does the same: it speaks of God's hands, His face and His throne. If those words are acceptable in the Quran, the argument runs, Muslims cannot fault them in the Bible.[1]

The Quran does use those words, and Muslims have discussed them for fourteen centuries. The question is whether the Bible's language is of the same kind, or goes further.

This article aims to provide context to that question, insha'Allah, in six passages from the Torah, each set beside the Bible's own correctives and the Quran's rule. That rule is one verse: "there is nothing whatever like unto Him, and He is the One that hears and sees (all things)" (42:11).[2]

"They heard Yahweh God's voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden" (Genesis 3:8).[3]

God moves through a place at a time of day, and the man and woman hide from Him among the trees. The Quran tells the same story and says only that their Lord called to them (7:22).[2]

"Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart" (Genesis 6:6). He says the same of Saul: "It grieves me that I have set up Saul to be king" (1 Samuel 15:11).[3]

The Bible answers itself. "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent" (Numbers 23:19), and in the very chapter about Saul: "the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent" (1 Samuel 15:29).[3] A reader has to choose which of the two statements governs the other.

Of Sodom and Gomorrah God says: "I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know" (Genesis 18:21).[3]

The verse speaks of God learning by going and looking. The Quran says of His knowledge: "He knoweth what (appeareth to His creatures as) before or after or behind them" (2:255).[2]

"Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day" (Genesis 32:24). He is renamed Israel, "for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed", and he says, "I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (32:28, 30).[3]

Jewish and Christian readers have long debated who the wrestler was: an angel, a manifestation of God, or, for many Christian commentators, the Word before the incarnation. On any reading, the text says that a man fought God through a night and prevailed.

"In six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed" (Exodus 31:17). The next verse gives Moses tablets "written with God's finger" (31:18).[3]

The Quran answers the idea of divine rest directly: "We created the heavens and the earth and all between them in Six Days, nor did any sense of weariness touch Us" (50:38). Of the Throne it says that "He feeleth no fatigue in guarding and preserving them" (2:255).[2]

"Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11). Nine verses later God says, "You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live", and then, "I will take away my hand, and you will see my back; but my face shall not be seen" (33:20, 23).[3]

Moses Maimonides, the great Jewish philosopher, read such words as figures: the Torah "speaks in the language of men", the "face" is God's presence or essence, and the "back" is what follows from His acts.[4] His reading is a denial that God has a body, and it is the same denial the Quran makes.

The bottom line

The Quran speaks of God's hands, face and throne, and Muslims affirm them as God describes Himself, "without asking how" (bilā kayf), with no likening of God to creatures and no emptying of the words, as al-Fārūqī sets out al-Ashʿarī's position.[5] We set out those verses in our article on God's hand, face and throne in the Quran.

The Torah passages go further than attributes. They tell of a God who walks in a garden, regrets, goes down to learn, is wrestled through a night, rests and is refreshed, and is seen face to face, and the Bible's own correctives in Numbers 23:19 and Exodus 33:20 deny each of these. The Quran's verse is the measure both readers need: "there is nothing whatever like unto Him" (42:11).[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The reply is common in Christian apologetics addressed to Muslims; the Bismikaa archive discussed the subject in its articles on the attributes of God.
  2. Quran 42:11; 7:22; 2:255; 50:38, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Genesis 3:8; 6:6; 18:20 to 21; 32:22 to 32; Exodus 31:17 to 18; 33:11 to 23; Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:11, 29, 35 (World English Bible).
  4. Moses Maimonides, The Guide of the Perplexed, part 1, chapters 26, 37 and 38.
  5. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 2.
